modules.title: Being an RSS practitioner
modules.intro: You represent RSS every time you walk into a nursery. This module sets out what the setting expects from you, what RSS expects from you, and the lines you never cross.
modules.body:
Resourceful Staffing Support | Part of Resourceful Ruth

You represent RSS every time you walk into a nursery. This module sets out what the setting expects from you, what RSS expects from you, and the professional boundaries you must maintain.

Our expectation is simple: be reliable, be professional and put children’s safety first.

Your role

RSS supplies temporary and casual cover to nurseries. During each shift, you work under the day-to-day direction of the setting’s manager and room leader.

Follow that setting’s policies and reasonable instructions, even where its routines differ from another nursery’s, provided they are safe, lawful and within your training and competence.

Your assignment is arranged through RSS. The setting directs your work during the shift, while RSS remains your contact for bookings, attendance, assignment issues and concerns.

If an instruction appears unsafe or conflicts with safeguarding requirements, pause the task where safe, explain your concern and seek guidance. Never leave children without appropriate supervision while resolving an issue.

Before every shift

  • Confirm the booking, the address, start time and who to report to.
  • Bring photo ID and your DBS details (Update Service number if you have one). Settings are entitled to see them.
  • Plan to arrive 10 minutes early. If you will be late or are unwell, call RSS straight away. Do not rely on a text or contact the nursery’s parents’ line..
  • Dress for floor work: clean, plain, practical clothing and closed flat shoes. No long dangling jewellery, no false nails, hair tied back.

  • Make sure you know how to contact RSS during your shift and where to find its safeguarding and whistleblowing procedures.

Your arrival checklist (ask if nobody tells you)

Complete this at every setting. Do not assume the arrangements are the same as at your previous nursery.

  1. Sign in on the staff register and show ID.
  2. Find out who is the Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) on duty today, and who is the deputy DSL.
  3. Find out who the paediatric first aider is, where first-aid supplies are kept and how to summon help.
  4. Learn the fire exits, assembly point and how the alarm sounds.
  5. Ask how accidents, incidents and safeguarding concerns are reported and recorded.
  6. Ask where the allergy and dietary list is for your room and read it before any food comes out. 
  7. Ask about individual care plans, additional needs and medical information relevant to the children you will support.
  8. Confirm the arrangements for toileting, nappy changing, sleep supervision and infection prevention.
  9. Ask about headcounts, room transitions, outdoor supervision and handovers.
  10. Ask how authorised collection is checked and what your role is at collection time.
  11. Hand in or securely store your phone, smartwatch and bag as the setting directs.
  12. Hand in or lock away your phone, smartwatch and bag as the setting directs.
  13. Ask the room leader for the routine, any children with additional needs, and who can collect whom.

  14. Tell the room leader about any limits to your training or experience before accepting a task.s

Always
  • Follow the room leader's direction and the setting's policies
  • Get down to children's level and join their play

  • Stay actively engaged and position yourself so you can supervise effectively.

  • Respect children’s dignity, privacy, individual needs and backgrounds

  • Respect children’s dignity, privacy, individual needs and backgrounds

  • Ask for help when you are unsure

  • Report concerns the same shift, in writing
  • Keep everything about children and families confidential
  • Get your timesheet signed by the manager before you leave
  • Tell RSS about any incident, accident or concern involving you
Never
  • Use your phone or take photos in the setting
  • Post about children, families or the nursery online, even without names
  • Give parents your number or social media, or arrange private babysitting with families you meet through RSS
  • Release a child to anyone without the manager's say-so

  • Leave children or an allocated supervision duty without a clear handover

  • Leave early or swap shifts without RSS and the manager agreeing
  • Accept a direct job or shift offer from a setting without telling RSS

  • Carry out a task you have not been trained, briefed or authorised to undertake.

  • Photograph records, take confidential records home or store work information on a personal device

  • Ignore unsafe practice because you are “only agency staff”

Safeguarding comes first 

Know how to contact the DSL or deputy immediately.

If a child is at immediate risk, take urgent action to protect them and obtain emergency help where needed. Do not wait for RSS to respond before taking necessary safeguarding action.

If a child tells you something concerning

  • Listen calmly and take them seriously.
  • Do not promise secrecy.
  • Do not ask leading questions or investigate yourself.
  • Report the concern immediately through the setting’s safeguarding procedure.
  • Record what you saw or heard factually, including the child’s own words where possible.

If you are concerned about an adult’s conduct
Report concerns about an adult’s behaviour, unsafe practice or possible harm to a child through the setting’s safeguarding or allegations procedure. Tell RSS promptly through its agreed reporting route.

If the concern involves the manager, DSL or your usual RSS contact, use the alternative reporting route in the relevant safeguarding or whistleblowing procedure.

Do not assume someone else has reported a concern. If you believe a concern has not been acted on, escalate it. You do not need permission from RSS to contact an appropriate safeguarding authority.

Informing RSS does not replace reporting to the setting or taking urgent safeguarding action.

Reporting accidents, incidents and concerns

Report safeguarding concerns, injuries, missing children, unsafe practice and immediate risks straight away to the appropriate person. Do not wait until the end of your shift.

Once immediate safety needs have been addressed:

  1. Follow the setting’s reporting and recording procedure.
  2. Make a clear, factual record as soon as it is safe to do so.
  3. Include what happened, when and where it happened, who was present, what action was taken and who was informed.
  4. Separate what you personally saw or heard from information someone else gave you.
  5. Tell RSS promptly through its agreed reporting route where the matter involves you or raises a significant concern about the assignment.

Do not investigate, speculate, alter records or ask colleagues to leave information out.

Supervision and handovers

Stay actively engaged with the children you are supporting.

Before taking a break, changing rooms, leaving an allocated duty or finishing your shift, tell the room leader and complete a clear handover to the appropriate colleague.

Raise concerns immediately if you believe children are not being safely supervised or you are being given responsibilities beyond your competence.

Do not simply walk away and leave children without care. Seek immediate support and follow the appropriate escalation procedure.

Before you leave

  • Hand over any outstanding information to the room leader or manager.
  • Check that required records have been completed and submitted.
  • Make sure urgent concerns have been reported, not simply written down.
  • Sign out and return any keys, passes or equipment.
  • Contact RSS about any significant issue that needs follow-up, using the agreed reporting route.

Work within your competence

Only undertake tasks for which you have the necessary training, setting-specific briefing and authorisation. This includes:

  • Administering medicines.
  • Nappy changing, toileting and other intimate care.
  • Supporting individual medical needs.
  • Taking children off-site.
  • Using unfamiliar equipment.
  • Carrying out designated first-aid responsibilities.

Be honest about your qualifications, experience and whether your training is current.

If you have not been shown the procedure or are unsure what is expected, say so before starting. Do not guess or copy what happened at another nursery.

“I haven’t been shown that yet — please talk me through your procedure” is professional, not awkward. 

Professional boundaries and direct offers of work

Be friendly and approachable while keeping relationships professional.

Do not share personal contact details with families or use an RSS assignment to arrange private childcare or babysitting.

If a setting approaches you about direct shifts or permanent employment, tell RSS promptly so any contractual arrangements can be handled correctly.

Do not independently change an existing RSS booking or agree to an assignment change without involving RSS.

Confidentiality and data

Information about children, families and colleagues is confidential. Some information, including health information, has additional legal protection.

Access and share information only where necessary for your role, safeguarding or another authorised purpose.

  • Discuss a child only with people who need the information for their work or an authorised safeguarding purpose.
  • Do not discuss confidential matters in front of other parents, visitors or people who do not need to know.
  • Use approved systems and reporting routes.
  • Do not photograph records, save information on personal devices or use personal messaging accounts to share confidential information.
  • Do not take records or personal notes about children home.
  • Complete and store records using the setting’s approved system.
  • Where RSS needs information, use RSS’s agreed secure reporting route and share only what is necessary.

Confidentiality must never prevent you from reporting a safeguarding concern to the appropriate person or authority.

Under UK GDPR, information about children and families is personal data, and some of it (health, SEND, safeguarding) is special category data. Only discuss a child with staff who need to know, never in front of other parents, and never outside the building. Don't take notes home. If you write anything down at work, it stays at work.

quiz.q: You are running 20 minutes late for a 7:30 shift. What do you do first?
o: Text the room leader you met last week
Call RSS immediately so they can warn the setting and arrange cover if needed
Message the nursery's parent WhatsApp group
Just arrive as quickly as possible
quiz.w: RSS manages your booking and must know first, so ratios can be protected.

quiz.q: A parent you got on well with asks for your number to do some weekend babysitting. What is the right response?
o: Give it, it's your free time
Give it only if the manager isn't around
Politely decline and mention it to RSS
quiz.w: Private arrangements with families met through placements blur professional boundaries and breach RSS terms.

quiz.q: Which of these should you find out within your first few minutes at a new setting?
o: Who the DSL is today and where the allergy list is
Where the staff room biscuits are
quiz.w: You must know who to report safeguarding concerns to and which children have allergies before working with them.

quiz.q: Where should your phone be during your shift?
o: Wherever the setting's policy says, which is normally locked away out of the rooms
On the windowsill so you can hear it
quiz.w: EYFS 2025 requires safeguarding policies to cover mobile phones and cameras; follow the setting's rules.

quiz.q: You notice the setting does something differently from another nursery you worked at. Whose procedure do you follow?
o: The other nursery's, it was better
This setting's policy, and raise any genuine safety concern with the manager
quiz.w: You work under the setting's policies. Raise safety concerns; don't freelance.

modules.title: EYFS 2025 essentials
modules.intro: The Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) is the statutory framework every registered nursery in England must follow. The current version took effect on 1 September 2025.
modules.body:
What the EYFS covers

The framework has three parts: the learning and development requirements, the assessment requirements and the safeguarding and welfare requirements. Nurseries are inspected against it by Ofsted. As cover staff you mostly touch learning through play and the welfare requirements, which are the ones that keep children safe.

Four overarching principles

  • A unique child: every child is constantly learning and can be resilient, capable, confident and self-assured.
  • Positive relationships: children learn to be strong and independent through warm, consistent relationships.
  • Enabling environments: environments and adults respond to each child's needs and interests.
  • Learning and development: children develop and learn at different rates, including children with SEND.

Seven areas of learning

Prime areasSpecific areas
Communication and languageLiteracy
Physical developmentMathematics
Personal, social and emotional developmentUnderstanding the world
Expressive arts and design

The prime areas matter most for the youngest children. For babies and toddlers, your talk, songs, eye contact and turn-taking are the curriculum.

Characteristics of effective teaching and learning

  • Playing and exploring: investigating and having a go
  • Active learning: concentrating, keeping on trying, enjoying achievements
  • Creating and thinking critically: having their own ideas and making links

The key person

Every child has a key person who builds a close bond with them and their family. As cover, you support the key person's work: pass on anything a parent tells you, and anything you notice, to that child's key person or the room leader.

What changed in EYFS 2025 (and why it matters to you)

  • Safer recruitment: references must be obtained before staff start, and safeguarding policies must describe safer recruitment. Expect settings to check your ID and DBS.
  • Safeguarding training (Annex C): sets out what training must cover; it must be refreshed at least every two years.
  • The Designated Safeguarding Lead replaces the old "lead practitioner" wording.
  • Safer eating: stronger rules on supervision, allergies and choking (Module 7).
  • Toileting and nappy changing: children's privacy must be balanced with safeguarding (Module 5).
  • Whistleblowing: every provider must have a whistleblowing policy (Module 4).
  • Child absence: settings must follow up absences promptly and hold at least two emergency contacts.
This course is RSS's induction. It does not replace a full accredited safeguarding course or a paediatric first aid certificate. RSS will tell you which of those you need for the rooms you work in.

quiz.q: Which are the three PRIME areas of learning?
o: Communication and language; Physical development; Personal, social and emotional development
quiz.w: The prime areas underpin everything else, especially for under-3s.

quiz.q: From what date did the current EYFS framework take effect?
quiz.w: EYFS 2025 came into force on 1 September 2025.

quiz.q: A parent tells you at drop-off that their child had a bad night. What should you do?
o: Tell the child's key person or room leader
quiz.w: Key person relationships depend on information being passed on.

quiz.q: Under EYFS 2025, how often must safeguarding training be refreshed as a minimum?
quiz.w: Annex C sets the content and training must be updated at least every two years.

quiz.q: Which is a characteristic of effective teaching and learning?
quiz.w: The three characteristics are playing and exploring, active learning, and creating and thinking critically.

modules.title: Safeguarding & child protection
modules.intro: Safeguarding is everyone's responsibility, including temporary staff on their first day. This module has a 100% pass mark.
modules.body:
The four categories of abuse

CategoryPossible signs in young children
PhysicalUnexplained bruises, especially on soft areas (cheeks, ears, upper arms, torso), bruising on non-mobile babies, burns, fearfulness, flinching
EmotionalVery withdrawn or "frozen" watchfulness, excessive clinginess or no attachment at all, delayed speech, harsh words from carers
SexualSexualised play or language beyond their age, soreness or injury in the genital area, fear of nappy changing or a particular adult
NeglectPersistent hunger, poor hygiene, untreated nappy rash or medical needs, unsuitable clothing for the weather, frequent unexplained absence

Also be alert to domestic abuse at home, child-on-child harm, female genital mutilation (FGM), radicalisation (the Prevent duty), children missing from education or care, and exploitation of older siblings. A single sign proves nothing; a pattern, or something a child says, must always be passed on.

If a child tells you something

  1. Stay calm and listen. Let the child speak in their own words. Show you are listening and that they did the right thing telling you.
  2. Do not ask leading questions such as "Did Daddy hurt you?". If you need to, use open prompts like "Tell me more".
  3. Never promise to keep it secret. Say you will need to tell someone whose job is to keep them safe.
  4. Do not investigate, examine the child, or confront the parent.
  5. Tell the DSL straight away, the same shift, before you leave the building.
  6. Write it down on the setting's form: date, time, what you saw, the child's exact words, who was present. Facts, not opinions. Sign it.
  7. Let RSS know you have raised a concern (no detail over text or WhatsApp).
If a child is in immediate danger, call 999. If the DSL is unavailable or you think they have not acted, you can contact the local authority children's social care team directly. Anyone can make a referral.

Concerns about an adult

If you are worried about how a member of staff, a student or another agency worker treats children, tell the manager. If the concern is about the manager, go to the owner or the Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO). The setting must tell Ofsted about allegations against staff. If an allegation is made about you, RSS will be informed and will support the process; do not contact the family or discuss it with colleagues.

Protecting yourself and the children

  • Until a setting has confirmed your suitability checks, you must not have unsupervised contact with children.
  • Stay visible. Keep doors open where policy says so and avoid being alone with a child out of sight of others.
  • No favourites, no gifts, no secrets with children. No physical contact a child doesn't want. Comfort is fine; follow the child's lead and the setting's policy.

quiz.q: A three-year-old tells you 'Mummy's boyfriend hits me but it's a secret.' What do you say?
o: 'Did he hit you with his hand or a belt?'
'You did the right thing telling me. I'm going to tell someone whose job is to help keep you safe.'
'That's not a nice thing to say about someone.'
quiz.w: Reassure, don't question, never promise secrecy.

quiz.q: When must you report a safeguarding concern to the DSL?
o: At the end of the week
Straight away, the same shift, before you leave
Only if you are sure abuse is happening
quiz.w: Delays put children at risk. You don't need proof to report.

quiz.q: What should your written record contain?
o: Date, time, what you saw and the child's exact words, signed
A guess at who did it
quiz.w: Factual, timed, signed records using the child's own words.

quiz.q: You see a bruise on a baby who is not yet crawling. What do you do?
o: Ask the parent at pick-up how it happened
Report it to the DSL straight away and record it
quiz.w: Bruising on non-mobile babies is a significant indicator. Report it; never photograph on a personal device.

quiz.q: You are worried about the way the nursery manager speaks to children. Who could you go to?
o: The owner/provider or the LADO, and tell RSS
quiz.w: Concerns about a manager go above them: the provider or the LADO.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four categories of abuse?
quiz.w: The four categories are physical, emotional, sexual abuse and neglect.

modules.title: Whistleblowing & raising concerns
modules.intro: EYFS 2025 makes a written whistleblowing policy mandatory for every provider. It covers you as agency staff too. 100% pass mark.
modules.body:
What whistleblowing is

Whistleblowing means raising a concern about wrongdoing or poor practice in the workplace that puts children or others at risk: unsafe ratios, staff not following safeguarding procedures, falsified records, or covering up an incident. It is different from a personal grievance about your own pay or hours.

How to raise a concern

  1. Raise it with the room leader or manager first, unless they are involved.
  2. If that doesn't work or isn't safe, go to the owner/provider, and tell RSS.
  3. If you still have concerns, go outside the organisation: Ofsted's whistleblowing line (0300 123 3155), the LADO, or the NSPCC Whistleblowing Advice Line (0800 028 0285).
You are legally protected when you raise a genuine concern in the public interest, even if you turn out to be mistaken. RSS will never penalise you for raising a concern in good faith, and will stop placing you at a setting if you are treated badly for doing so.

Low-level concerns

Not every worry is a crisis. A colleague shouting, ignoring a crying baby, or using their phone in the room are "low-level" but still need to be raised. Patterns of small concerns are often how serious harm is spotted early.

quiz.q: The room is over ratio and the room leader tells you not to mention it. What should you do?
o: Raise it with the manager and tell RSS
quiz.w: Unsafe ratios put children at risk; this is a whistleblowing concern.

quiz.q: Which number is the NSPCC Whistleblowing Advice Line?
quiz.w: 0800 028 0285 is the NSPCC Whistleblowing Advice Line.

quiz.q: You raise a genuine concern that turns out to be unfounded. What happens?
o: You are protected because you acted in good faith
quiz.w: Good-faith concerns in the public interest are protected.

quiz.q: Which of these is a whistleblowing concern rather than a personal grievance?
o: Your shift was shorter than booked
Staff are signing children's medicine forms they didn't witness
quiz.w: Falsifying records puts children at risk.

modules.title: Intimate care, privacy & devices
modules.intro: Nappy changing and toileting are where safeguarding and dignity meet. EYFS 2025 now requires settings to balance children's privacy with safeguarding. 100% pass mark.
modules.body:
Doing intimate care well

  • Follow the setting's intimate care policy. On a first shift, ask whether you may change nappies alone or should work alongside a permanent member of staff.
  • Tell a colleague when you are taking a child to change or toilet them.
  • Talk the child through what you are doing. Ask before you touch ("I'm going to wipe you now, is that OK?") and encourage them to do what they can.
  • Give privacy from other children and visitors: use the changing area, close screens or partial doors as policy says, but never in a way that hides you from staff.
  • Wear gloves and an apron, follow hygiene procedures and complete the changing record.
  • Report any marks, soreness or unusual behaviour to the room leader and DSL.

Phones, cameras and smart devices

Settings' safeguarding policies must cover mobile phones and cameras. As RSS staff:

Do
  • Lock your phone and smartwatch away as directed
  • Use only the setting's devices for photos, and only if asked
  • Give the setting's landline to anyone who might need to reach you in an emergency
Don't
  • Take any photo or video of children on your own device, ever
  • Wear a smartwatch with a camera in rooms
  • Share or forward images from the setting's app

Online conduct

Don't name the setting, post in uniform, or describe "a funny thing a child did today". Don't accept friend requests from parents. Even anonymised posts can identify children.

quiz.q: It's your first shift. A toddler needs changing and the room leader is busy. What do you do?
o: Change them alone in the staff toilet with the door shut
Check the setting's policy and ask whether you may change alone or should work with a colleague
Ask a parent to do it
quiz.w: Follow the intimate care policy; on day one, confirm what you may do.

quiz.q: How does EYFS 2025 describe privacy during nappy changing?
o: Privacy must be balanced with safeguarding considerations
Children must always be changed in front of the whole room
quiz.w: The change: respect dignity and privacy, but never at the cost of safeguarding.

quiz.q: A parent asks you to take a photo of their child's painting on your phone. Do you?
o: No, never use your personal device for photos in the setting
Yes, if you delete it later
Only if no other children are in it
quiz.w: No personal devices for images, without exception.

quiz.q: Before a nappy change you should:
o: Tell a colleague and talk the child through it
Take the child somewhere out of sight
Change them on the floor in the main room
quiz.w: Visibility to staff plus communication with the child.

modules.title: Ratios & supervision
modules.intro: Ratios are a legal minimum, not a target. Agency cover is usually booked precisely to keep a room in ratio, so it matters where you are and what you are doing.
modules.body:
Minimum staff:child ratios (group settings, EYFS 2025)

Age of childrenRatioNotes
Under 21 : 3At least one member of staff holds a full and relevant Level 3; at least half have received training specific to babies
Aged 21 : 5At least one member of staff holds a full and relevant Level 3
3 and over1 : 81 : 13 can apply when a person with Qualified Teacher Status (or equivalent) is working directly with the children

The manager decides whether you count in ratio, based on your checks, qualifications and experience. Ask on arrival: "Am I counted in ratio today, and for which room?"

Supervision in practice

  • Never leave children unsupervised, even for a moment. If you need to leave the room, tell a colleague and wait for them to take over.
  • Position yourself so you can see the whole space, with your back to the wall rather than the room.
  • Count children at every transition: going outside, coming in, before and after lunch, at sleep time.
  • Children who are sleeping must be checked regularly. Babies are always placed on their backs to sleep.
  • Never let a child leave with anyone not on their authorised collection list, even if they say they are family. Get the manager.

quiz.q: What is the minimum ratio for under-2s?
quiz.w: 1 adult to 3 children under 2.

quiz.q: What is the minimum ratio for 2-year-olds in a group setting?
quiz.w: 1:5 for children aged two (since September 2024, retained in EYFS 2025).

quiz.q: You urgently need the toilet and are alone with four 2-year-olds. What do you do?
o: Call or signal a colleague and wait until they take over
Ask the oldest child to watch the others
quiz.w: Never leave children unsupervised.

quiz.q: How should a baby be placed to sleep?
quiz.w: Back to sleep reduces the risk of sudden infant death.

quiz.q: A man says he's the child's uncle and has come to collect her. He isn't on the list. What do you do?
o: Let her go, she seems happy to see him
Keep the child with you and fetch the manager
Ask him for ID and then release her
Call the child's mother yourself on your mobile
quiz.w: Only authorised adults collect. The manager handles any change, using the setting's procedure.

modules.title: Safer eating, allergies & hygiene
modules.intro: Choking and allergic reactions are among the most serious risks in nursery. EYFS 2025 strengthened the safer-eating requirements.
modules.body:
Safer eating rules

  • Children must be within sight and hearing of a member of staff whenever they eat.
  • At least one member of staff with a full paediatric first aid certificate must be in the room when children are eating.
  • Children must be sat down to eat and drink, never walking, running or lying down.
  • Food is prepared to suit each child's age and stage: whole grapes, cherry tomatoes, blueberries and similar round foods are cut lengthways into quarters; sausages cut lengthways; no whole nuts.
  • Babies are never left propped with a bottle.

Allergies and dietary needs

  1. Read the room's allergy and dietary list before any food or drink appears, including snacks, cooking and messy play (pasta, flour, cereals).
  2. Check every plate against the list. If unsure, don't give it; ask.
  3. Know which children have an adrenaline auto-injector or inhaler, where it is kept, and who is trained to use it.
  4. Don't share food from your own lunch with children, ever.
Signs of anaphylaxis: swelling of lips, tongue or throat; difficulty breathing or a hoarse voice; wheeze; sudden paleness or floppiness. Shout for help, get the first aider and auto-injector, and call 999.

Hygiene

Wash hands before handling food, after nappy changes and toileting, after outdoor play and after wiping noses. Help children wash theirs. Report illness: children with sickness or diarrhoea are normally excluded for 48 hours after the last episode. Follow the setting's rules for you too.

quiz.q: During lunch, what does EYFS 2025 require?
o: Children are within sight and hearing of staff, seated, with a paediatric first aider in the room
quiz.w: Sight and hearing, seated, PFA-trained staff in the room.

quiz.q: How should grapes be prepared for a two-year-old?
o: Cut in half across the middle
quiz.w: Quartering lengthways removes the round shape that blocks airways.

quiz.q: When should you check the allergy list?
o: Before any food, drink or food-based play is offered
quiz.w: Including snacks, cooking and messy play materials.

quiz.q: A child's lips start swelling and they are wheezing after snack. Your first actions?
o: Shout for help, get the first aider and auto-injector, call 999
Put them down for a nap
quiz.w: Treat suspected anaphylaxis as an emergency.

quiz.q: Can you share your own snack with a child who asks nicely?
o: Only if the parent is there
quiz.w: You can't know every allergy or dietary need.

modules.title: Accidents, medicines & emergencies
modules.intro: Things will go wrong sometimes. What matters is a calm, correct response and an accurate record.
modules.body:
Accidents and injuries

  • Get the first aider if you are not trained. Stay with the child.
  • Every accident is recorded, and parents are told the same day or as soon as reasonably practicable.
  • Note any existing injury a child arrives with on the setting's existing-injury form, not the accident form.
  • Head bumps always get reported to the room leader and recorded, even if the child seems fine.

Medicines

Only give medicine if you have been trained and asked by the manager. Settings must have written parental permission for each medicine and keep a record each time it is given. Prescription medicines are only given if prescribed for that child by a doctor, dentist, nurse or pharmacist.

Behaviour and physical intervention

Physical punishment is never used or threatened, and nor is anything that humiliates or frightens a child. Physical intervention is only used to prevent immediate danger or injury, and must be recorded and the parent told the same day.

Emergencies

  1. Fire: on the alarm, take your group out by the nearest exit, take the register if it's yours to carry, go to the assembly point, count children. Never go back in.
  2. Lockdown: follow the manager's instruction, keep children calm and quiet away from windows.
  3. Missing child: raise the alarm immediately to the manager. Don't wait to search alone.

quiz.q: A child falls in the garden and bumps their head. They seem fine. What do you do?
o: Tell the room leader, make sure it's recorded and the parent is told
Put a plaster on and move on
quiz.w: Head bumps are always recorded and reported; parents informed the same day.

quiz.q: The room leader asks you to give a child Calpol. You haven't been trained and haven't seen the consent form. You:
o: Explain you aren't trained in their procedure and ask a trained colleague to do it
Ask the child how much they usually have
quiz.w: Only trained staff with written permission give medicine, and it's recorded.

quiz.q: When can staff physically restrain a child?
o: To prevent immediate danger or injury, then record and inform parents the same day
quiz.w: Physical intervention only to prevent harm; always recorded and reported.

quiz.q: During a fire evacuation you realise your water bottle is inside. You:
o: Stay at the assembly point with the children
Ask a child to fetch it
Go back once the alarm quietens
quiz.w: Never re-enter a building on fire.

modules.title: Play, learning & inclusion
modules.intro: Good cover staff don't just watch children; they play, talk and help them learn, and they make every child feel welcome.
modules.body:
Quality interactions

  • Get down to children's level. Follow their interests rather than directing the play.
  • Use the "observe, wait, listen" approach: notice what a child is doing, pause, then join in.
  • Narrate and expand: if a child says "car", you might say "a red car, it's going fast!".
  • Ask open questions ("What do you think will happen?") and give time to answer.
  • Sing, read and share rhymes. Repetition is how young children learn language.

Supporting behaviour

Young children are still learning to manage big feelings. Stay calm, name the feeling ("You're cross because Sam took the truck"), give simple choices, and praise what you want to see. Follow the setting's behaviour policy and any individual plans. Never shout, shame or use food as a reward or punishment.

Inclusion, SEND and EAL

  • Ask the room leader about children with SEND: their communication method, triggers, sensory needs and any one-to-one support.
  • Use the child's preferred name, correctly pronounced.
  • For children learning English as an additional language, use gesture, pictures and simple repeated words; their home language is a strength, not a problem.
  • Respect families' cultures, faiths and routines (food, clothing, hair care, sleep).

Observations

If the setting asks you to note something a child did, write what you saw and heard, factually, and pass it to the key person. Don't add to children's records on apps unless you are given access and shown how.

o: 'Yes, a big brown dog! He's wagging his tail.'

Bite them back to show it hurts

o: Use gestures, pictures and simple repeated words and value their home language
quiz.w: Home language supports learning English.

o: 'What do you think will happen if we add water?'
quiz.w: Open questions invite thinking and longer answers.
